An adjoining-owner agreement about accretion must be registered to have effect.
Legal presumptions may help where deeds are unclear but can be rebutted by other evidence.
A red edging may be altered to better reflect a presumption, but the boundary remains general.
An alteration application must identify the presumption, include a plan, and include relevant pre-registration documents.
Legal presumptions cannot alter a boundary determined under section 60.
Land abutting a road may be presumed to include soil to the road's middle line, subject to rebuttal.
For a hedge or bank with an artificial ditch, the presumed boundary is the far edge of the ditch.
The hedge-and-ditch presumption does not apply to natural ditches or features created during common ownership.
A natural non-tidal stream boundary is presumed to follow the centre line, subject to rebuttal.
A lake wholly within one ownership belongs to that owner; otherwise no general presumption is stated.
Absent contrary evidence, land adjoining the sea ends at the top of the foreshore.
Foreshore is presumed Crown-owned unless evidence shows otherwise.
Foundations or eaves extending beyond a ground-level line may be included unless contrary evidence exists.
Vertical ownership is presumed to include necessary airspace and subsoil, subject to exclusions.
